Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I put on loud music or TV
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
People are not what they seem
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette:
Mariana, a 34-year-old prison guard, had not spoken about what happened to her in her home country for nearly fifteen years. She had fled with her family during a period of political violence when she was still a teenager. The night they tried to cross the border, a group of soldiers stopped them. The men smelled sharply of alcohol, their voices overlapping as they shouted orders in a language Mariana understood all too well. One soldier grabbed her mother by the arm and screamed for her father to kneel. Mariana could still hear that voice in her head when the memory came back—the exact pitch, the slur at the end of each word, the sound of boots scraping on gravel. The images were so vivid that she could describe the stitching on the soldier’s uniform collar, the sweat on his upper lip. When the memory returned, it came with a wave of emotion that felt as raw as the moment itself—terror so thick she had to stop whatever she was doing, press her hands to her face, and wait for it to recede.

After resettling in the United States, Mariana had worked hard to build a life. She married a kind man who knew nothing of that night. She took a job as a prison guard because it offered stability and a sense of purpose, even though every day she found herself surrounded by the very things that could undo her. The smell of alcohol on an inmate’s breath during a routine count made her chest tighten and her vision narrow. When a supervisor issued a direct order—even a reasonable one—she felt a jolt of dread that she could not explain. She had come to believe that uniforms signaled danger, that people in authority were not what they seemed, and that the world was fundamentally unsafe. She no longer recognised herself: the Mariana who had once been open and trusting had become someone who looked for threats in every glance, every sudden movement. She was certain she had lost something essential, and she did not know how to get it back.

The symptoms bled into every part of her life. At work, she chose her seat in the break room based on where she felt most protected—back to the wall, a clear view of the door, an exit within reach. If a colleague moved suddenly behind her, she would flinch and brace for danger, heart pounding, even when nothing was wrong. She began avoiding certain supervisors, taking longer routes to avoid passing their offices, volunteering for shifts when fewer uniforms were around. At home, she put on loud music or the television at full volume, not for entertainment but to drown out the sounds that played in her head. Her husband complained that they could never have a quiet evening. When they went out to dinner, Mariana insisted on sitting in the corner, facing the room, and she scanned every table for anyone in uniform. She had taken to rehearsing escape routes from restaurants, movie theaters, even her own living room. Late at night, lying awake, she dwelled on how she could have prevented that night fifteen years ago—if she had pulled her mother faster, if she had hidden behind the car instead of standing in the open, if she had screamed louder. The rumination left her exhausted and hollow.

The turning point came on an ordinary afternoon at the prison. A correctional officer she did not know well placed a hand on her shoulder from behind to get her attention. Mariana spun around, her arm raised defensively, her breath coming in short gasps. She shouted something—she could not recall what—and the officer stepped back, startled. Her supervisor pulled her aside and asked if she was fit for duty. Mariana realised she had been teetering on the edge for months. That evening, she told her husband about the memories she had never shared, and he encouraged her to finally seek help. What she wanted, more than anything, was to stop feeling like a stranger to herself. She was afraid of what she might become if she did not face the past, but she was even more afraid of losing the life she had worked so hard to build.
